_meta.descricao: The "last things": death, particular judgment, the Last Judgment, heaven, hell, and purgatory.
_meta.aviso: Introductory doctrinal presentation on the ultimate destiny of man; for theological depth, consult the Catechism of the Catholic Church in its entirety.
_meta.revisao_editorial: The descriptions of Heaven, Hell, and Purgatory avoid literalism regarding symbolic biblical images (fire, darkness), following the caution of the Catechism itself.
fontes_gerais: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1005-1060

itens.resumo: For the Catholic faith, death brings to an end the earthly life of pilgrimage and free decision before God, with no possibility of a new choice after it.
itens.corpo: The Church teaches that death is the end of earthly existence, the close of the "single course of our earthly life" in which man decides, in the light of God, his eternal destiny — with no "reincarnation" or new chance to choose after death (Heb 9:27). Seen in the light of faith, Christian death is transformed by Christ: united to his death and resurrection, it ceases to be merely a biological end and becomes a passage — hence the Church speaks of the day of a saint's death as his "dies natalis", the day of birth into Heaven.
fontes: Hebrews 9:27
Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1005-1014

itens.resumo: The immediate judgment of each soul at the moment of death, which refers its life to Christ and decides its eternal destiny even before the final resurrection and the Last Judgment.
itens.corpo:
According to Catholic doctrine, each person is subjected, immediately after death, to a particular judgment before Christ, in which his immortal soul receives the eternal retribution corresponding to his faith and his works — either immediate entrance into the blessedness of Heaven (perhaps after purification in Purgatory) or eternal damnation. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (nos. 1021-1022) teaches that death puts an end to man's life as the time open to accepting or rejecting the divine grace manifested in Christ, and that each one receives "in his immortal soul eternal retribution at a particular judgment that refers his life to Christ". It is distinct from the Last Judgment, which will take place at the end of time and will also involve the resurrection of the bodies.

The biblical basis of this doctrine is found in the Letter to the Hebrews — "it is appointed for men to die once, and after that comes judgment" (Heb 9:27) — and in other passages that affirm an immediate and distinct destiny for each soul after death. The Catechism cites the parable of poor Lazarus (Lk 16:22), the word of Christ to the good thief on the cross — "today you will be with me in Paradise" (Lk 23:43) — and texts such as 2 Cor 5:8, Phil 1:23 and Heb 12:23. The same Catechism observes that, although the New Testament speaks of judgment primarily from the perspective of the final encounter with Christ at his second coming, it also repeatedly asserts the existence of an immediate retribution after death for each one. The doctrinal summary (no. 1051) states it succinctly: at death each man receives in his immortal soul his eternal retribution in a particular judgment by Christ, the judge of the living and the dead.

Historically, clarity about the particular judgment was linked to the definition of the state of souls before the resurrection. The constitution *Benedictus Deus*, of Pope Benedict XII (1336), in defining that the souls of the just already enjoy the beatific vision and that those of the damned descend immediately to perdition, presupposes and consolidates the doctrine of a judgment and a destiny fixed immediately after death — before the general judgment. The controversy with Pope John XXII (1316-1334), who seemed to postpone the vision of God until the end of time, was precisely the context in which this truth was solemnly affirmed.

The particular judgment is not, however, a second criterion independent of the Last Judgment: both reveal the same personal relationship with Christ. What distinguishes the particular judgment is its immediacy and its individual character, which definitively fix the soul's destiny at the moment of death, whereas the Last Judgment, at the second coming, will publicly manifest before all humanity the truth of each life. The liturgical prayer for the soul of the deceased — "may you see your Redeemer face to face" — expresses the faith that this contemplation is already decided at the passage from this life.

itens.resumo: The universal and definitive judgment of all humanity at the end of time, coinciding with the resurrection of the dead and the glorious second coming of Christ.
itens.corpo:
Unlike the particular judgment of each soul, the Last Judgment is the universal judgment of all human history, which will take place at the glorious second coming of Christ — the "Parousia" — when the dead will rise in their bodies and each person will see publicly manifested the truth of his relationship with God. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (nos. 1038-1041) teaches that "the resurrection of all the dead, 'both of the just and the unjust'" (cf. Acts 24:15) will precede the Last Judgment, in the "hour when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth, those who have done good deeds, to the resurrection of life, but those who have done wicked deeds, to the resurrection of condemnation" (Jn 5:28-29).

The most famous biblical description of this judgment is the scene in Matthew 25:31-46: the Son of Man comes in his glory with all the angels, sits upon his throne, and separates the nations "as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats," pronouncing the decisive criterion in the works of mercy — giving food to the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick and the imprisoned — identifying himself with the least ones: "whatever you did for one of these least brothers of mine, you did for me." Saint Augustine, cited in the liturgy and in the exegetical tradition, comments that it will then be made manifest that the poor were placed on earth as bearers of good works to the treasury of Christ, so that what was not given to them is not found deposited with him.

The Catechism stresses two essential points. First, the Last Judgment will take place when Christ comes in glory, but "only the Father knows the day and the hour; only he determines the moment of its coming"; in it the definitive word on all of history will be pronounced, and human beings will understand the ultimate meaning of all creation and of the entire economy of salvation, seeing how God's justice triumphs over all injustices and how his love is stronger than death. Second, the message of the Last Judgment is not primarily one of terror, but a call to conversion while there is still "the acceptable time, the day of salvation" (2 Cor 6:2); it inspires holy fear of God, commits us to the justice of the Kingdom, and proclaims the "blessed hope" (Titus 2:13) of the Lord's return, who will come "to be glorified in his holy ones" (2 Thes 1:10).

This truth is inscribed in the Church's profession of faith, which confesses that Christ "will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end." The liturgical tradition gave it expression in the hymn *Dies irae*, attributed to the medieval Franciscan tradition and incorporated into the Requiem Mass, with its verses on the "day of wrath" on which the world will dissolve into ashes. In art, the scene has been depicted countless times — from Fra Angelico's *Last Judgment* to Michelangelo's fresco in the Sistine Chapel (1536-1541), which covers the altar wall of the Vatican chapel and gathers more than three hundred figures around Christ the judge. The Catechism also observes that at the end of time, the Kingdom of God will reach its fullness with the promise of "new heavens and a new earth" (cf. Rev 21:1), when God will be "all in all" (1 Cor 15:28).

itens.resumo: The full and definitive communion of life and love with the Most Holy Trinity, with Mary, the angels and all the saints — the beatific vision, supreme happiness and the ultimate end of man.
itens.corpo:
Heaven is not described by Catholic doctrine as a physical place in the ordinary sense, but as the supreme and definitive state of happiness: the communion of life and love with the Trinity, with the Virgin Mary, the angels and all the blessed. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (nos. 1023-1029) defines this condition as the "beatific vision": those who die in God's grace and friendship and are perfectly purified live forever with Christ and see God "as he is" (1 Jn 3:2), "face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). It is the intuitive and immediate knowledge of the divine essence itself, in which no creature can serve as an intermediary, and which surpasses all human capacity for understanding or imagination in this life.

This formulation was fixed above all by the apostolic constitution *Benedictus Deus*, of Pope Benedict XII, promulgated on January 29, 1336. In it the pope defines, with apostolic authority, that the souls of the just — those who died with nothing to be purified, or who have already been purified after death — "have seen and see the divine essence with an intuitive vision, and even face to face, with no creature intervening as an object of vision", and that this vision and enjoyment "continue without interruption and without end until the Last Judgment and from then on forever". The document also clarifies that, once this immediate vision has begun, the acts of faith and hope cease in the souls, since these theological virtues give way to direct contemplation.

*Benedictus Deus* was a response to a concrete controversy. Pope John XXII (1316-1334), before his election and later in his preaching — more as a private theologian than as a teacher of the magisterium —, had maintained that the souls of the saved would attain the vision of God only after the Last Judgment, a position close to the idea of a "sleep of the soul". This provoked a strong reaction from theologians, especially at the University of Paris, who accused it of being heretical. In a consistory of January 3, 1334, John XXII declared that he had never intended to define the question, and, before dying, he retracted and professed the belief that souls separated from their bodies already enjoy the beatific vision in Heaven. Benedict XII's definition ended the dispute and remains the reference text on the state of souls before the resurrection.

Catholic doctrine links Heaven to the hope of the resurrection: the blessedness of the soul will be completed, at the end of time, with the glorification of the body, endowed then with impassibility, brightness, agility and subtlety. At the same time, it stresses the relational character of Heaven: according to the Catechism (nos. 954-956), the blessed do not withdraw from those who are still pilgrims on earth, but intercede for them — the so-called communion of saints. And it adds that those who are in glory continue to fulfill with joy the will of God in regard to other men and all creation, reigning with Christ (cf. Rev 22:5). The liturgy, for its part, expresses this hope in the prayer for the dead, asking that the soul of the faithful "may contemplate face to face his Redeemer", as the Rite of Anointing of the Sick and of the commendation of the dying prays.

itens.resumo: A state of definitive and free self-exclusion from communion with God, the consequence of dying in unrepented mortal sin.
itens.corpo: The Church teaches the existence of hell and its eternity not as an arbitrary imposition by God, but as the consequence of the creature's own free and definitive rejection of communion with God — "dying in mortal sin without repenting" (Catechism, no. 1033). It is described in Scripture with symbolic images ("eternal fire," "outer darkness") that express the gravity of this definitive separation, rather than literal descriptions of its physical nature.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1033-1037

itens.resumo: The state of final purification for souls who die in God's grace but are still imperfectly purified, before entering the full vision of God.
itens.corpo: Purgatory is not, in Catholic doctrine, a "second hell" nor a second chance at conversion: it is the state — not necessarily a place in the spatial sense — of final purification for souls who die in friendship with God (certainly destined for Heaven), but who still bear the consequences of sins whose guilt has already been forgiven. The Church recommends suffrages for the dead (prayers, almsgiving, indulgences) as concrete help to these souls, with a biblical basis cited, among other passages, in 2 Maccabees 12:46.
fontes: 2 Maccabees 12:46
Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1030-1032

itens.titulo: The Parousia (the Second Coming of Christ)
itens.resumo: The glorious return of Christ at the end of time, when He will publicly judge the living and the dead — a day and hour that, according to the Catechism itself, no one knows.
itens.corpo:
Parousia comes from the Greek parousía ("coming", "presence") and designates the glorious return of Jesus Christ at the end of history, when He will publicly judge the living and the dead at the Last Judgment. Since the Ascension, the Catechism teaches, this coming is already imminent — but no one knows "the times or seasons which the Father has fixed by his own authority" (Acts 1:7): neither the day nor the hour has been revealed to anyone, not even to the angels.

The Church teaches that, before the Parousia, she will pass through a final trial that will shake the faith of many believers — a period of religious apostasy marked by the deception of an "Antichrist", a pseudo-messianic imposture in which man glorifies himself in place of God. Only after this final trial, and the definitive triumph of God over evil, will Christ come "on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory" (Mt 24:30).

itens.resumo: The article of the Creed that professes that the bodies of the dead will rise at the end of time, reunited with their souls for eternal life or condemnation.
itens.corpo:
The Christian Creed professes "the resurrection of the body" as a distinct article of faith, placed immediately before "life everlasting." The doctrine teaches that, at the end of time, the bodies of all who have died will be reunited with their souls, in the same way—though in an incomparably superior form—as the body of Christ truly rose on the third day. The Catechism explains that "what is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable" (cf. 1 Cor 15:42-44): it is a "spiritual body," transformed, and not a mere reanimation of the previous biological life.

Faith in the resurrection of the body is clearly distinct from any doctrine of reincarnation: the Church teaches that each person lives a single earthly existence, deciding in it his eternal destiny, and that the same body each one had in life—transfigured—will be reunited with the soul at the final judgment, whether for glory or for condemnation, according to the life each one has lived.

This hope is founded entirely on the resurrection of Christ, the "first fruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Cor 15:20): for Saint Paul, if Christ has not been raised, the Christian faith is in vain; but, having been raised, he guarantees the resurrection of all who are united to him.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 988-1019
1 Corinthians 15:12-44

itens.resumo: The last article of the Creed: full and definitive communion with God, to which man is called after death, judgment, and the resurrection of the body.
itens.corpo:
"I believe in life everlasting" is the last article of the Apostles' Creed and of the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed, and it sums up the hope toward which the whole Christian faith professed in the preceding articles converges. It is the full, definitive, and everlasting communion with the One and Triune God, promised to those who die in his grace and friendship — the same reality that tradition also designates by the names "heaven" or "beatific vision."

The Catechism teaches that, for the Christian who unites his death to that of Christ, to die is not the end but the passage to the definitive encounter with the Lord: for this reason the funeral liturgy accompanies the dying person with words of hope, commending his soul "to the place of peace" and "to the company of the Virgin Mary and of all the angels and saints." Eternal life is not merely the survival of the soul, but — after the resurrection of the body — the fullness of the whole human being, body and soul, glorified in God.

The expression "eternal life" does not designate a mere indefinite duration in time, but another quality of existence: participation, beyond time, in the very life of God, described by Scripture as seeing face to face (1 Cor 13:12) and as the state in which "God will wipe away every tear from their eyes" (Rev 21:4).
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1020-1050
1 Corinthians 13:12; Revelation 21:4

itens.titulo: New Heavens and a New Earth
itens.resumo: The eschatological hope that, at the end of time, the whole created universe will be transfigured and renewed, and not simply destroyed.
itens.corpo:
Beyond the personal destiny of each human being, Catholic eschatology also affirms a destiny for the material universe: citing the Second Letter of Saint Peter and the Book of Revelation, the Catechism teaches the hope of "new heavens and a new earth" (2 Pet 3:13; Rev 21:1), in which righteousness will dwell and God will be "all in all" (1 Cor 15:28).

This consummation, which tradition also calls the "restoration of all things" (cf. Acts 3:21), is not understood as the annihilation of the present world, but as its transfiguration: the visible universe itself, the Catechism teaches, is destined to be transformed, so that, freed from the corruptibility introduced by sin, it may be fully at the service of the just glorified in Christ.

In this context, the Church rejects millenarianism, the idea of an intermediate earthly reign of Christ before the definitive end, considering it a falsification of the future Kingdom, especially in its politicized form of secularized messianism. The Christian hope in the new heavens and the new earth is not a historical program to be accomplished within time, but the horizon that will be fulfilled only beyond history, at the Last Judgment.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1042-1050
2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1; 1 Corinthians 15:28

itens.resumo: The supreme religious deception which, according to the Catechism, will precede the glorious return of Christ, in the form of a pseudo-messianism in which man glorifies himself.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism teaches that, before Christ's coming, the Church must pass through a final trial that will shake the faith of many believers: the persecution that accompanies her pilgrimage on earth will unveil the "mystery of iniquity" in the form of a religious deception offering men an apparent solution to their problems at the price of apostasy from the truth. This supreme religious deception is that of the Antichrist, that is, of a pseudo-messianism by which man glorifies himself in place of God and of his Messiah who has come in the flesh (CCC 675).

The Catechism clarifies that this antichristian deception is already present in the world every time the claim is made to realize within history that messianic hope which can only be realized beyond history through the eschatological judgment: the Church has rejected even the modified forms of this falsification of the kingdom to come under the name of millenarianism, especially the "intrinsically perverse" political form of a secular messianism (CCC 676).

The Church will enter the glory of the kingdom only through this final Passover, when she will follow her Lord in his death and Resurrection: the kingdom will be fulfilled, then, not by a historic triumph of the Church through a progressive ascendancy, but by God's victory over the final unleashing of evil, which will cause his Bride to come down from heaven. God's triumph over the revolt of evil will take the form of the Last Judgment after the final cosmic upheaval of this passing world (CCC 677).
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 675-677

itens.resumo: A theological hypothesis, never defined as dogma, about the fate of children who die without Baptism; today the Church entrusts their salvation to the mercy of God.
itens.corpo:
The "limbo of infants" was, for centuries, a theological hypothesis developed by medieval authors to explain the fate of children who die without Baptism, having committed no personal sin but born with original sin: a state of natural happiness, without the beatific vision, but also without suffering. This hypothesis was never defined as a dogma of faith by the Church, always remaining one theological opinion among others, although widely spread in common teaching between the Middle Ages and the twentieth century.

In 2007, the International Theological Commission published, with the authorization of Pope Benedict XVI, the document "The Hope of Salvation for Infants Who Die Without Being Baptised", acknowledging that the hypothesis of limbo reflected an excessively restrictive view of salvation. The document concluded that there are "serious theological and liturgical grounds for hope" that these children are saved and attain the vision of God, entrusting them to the divine mercy, which desires that all men be saved (1 Tim 2:4) and which instituted Baptism without, for that reason, being limited to it in its own means of saving.

The document itself clarifies that it is not a pronouncement of the solemn Magisterium, and that the hypothesis of limbo remains a theologically possible opinion, although rarely proposed today; what the Church clearly affirms is trust in the mercy of God and the urgent recommendation to parents not to delay the Baptism of their children.
fontes: International Theological Commission, The Hope of Salvation for Infants Who Die Without Being Baptised (April 19, 2007)
